body_paragraphs: The overnight calm didn't survive contact with an actual overnight. The US launched what Iranian state media called a 'heavy wave' of new strikes, and for the first time in weeks the casualties moved from ships and infrastructure to named civilians - at least three dead inside Iran, one more in Kuwait, where an Iranian strike hit a Chinese-owned building. Trump's framing was blunt: 'it's our turn to hit them, very hard.' Whatever Tuesday's Trump-Netanyahu meeting implied about de-escalation, this is not that.

The Fed, meanwhile, did exactly what was expected and still managed to unsettle everyone. Nine members voted to hold rates at 3.50-3.75%; three, all regional bank presidents, wanted a hike instead. The market read the three-way split as confirmation that inflation risk is real and unresolved, not reassurance that it's contained - the S&P's worst day in weeks, the Nasdaq down more than 1.7%, yields rising on a hold rather than falling. Friday's jobs report is the next thing that actually moves this.

The Marlins gave the day its one clean good outcome: down 6-0, they came back to sweep the Phillies, their biggest comeback of the season, with three players nobody outside Miami has heard floated as trade bait each driving in runs that make them harder to deal before Monday's deadline. And if you want an evening a long way from vote counts and casualty counts: Vizcaya, a house built to look four hundred years old on the day it opened, or a re-read of the Sartre lecture on what it actually means to choose something for yourself.

beautiful_thing.title: Vizcaya
beautiful_thing.creator: F. Burrall Hoffman (architect), Diego Suárez (landscape architect), Paul Chalfin (artistic director)
beautiful_thing.body: Industrialist James Deering, a vice president of International Harvester, built Vizcaya on Biscayne Bay so that it would look, on the day it opened, like an Italian estate that had already stood for four hundred years. Deering and Chalfin toured Europe acquiring actual centuries-old doors, mantels, and ceilings to build that illusion into the structure itself. Colombian landscape architect Diego Suárez laid out the ten acres of formal gardens against a native rockland hammock. The estate was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1994 and is now a museum open to the public in Coconut Grove.

noticing_prompt.text: Notice how much of today's news arrived as a number standing in for something that happened to an actual person - a vote count, a percentage drop, a dollar figure per square foot - and pick one and ask what it actually cost someone.

daily_puzzle.prompt: A trader glances at the same stock ticker twice within the same minute and sees two different prices, even though the exchange's own records show that zero shares changed hands in between. Nothing is broken, delayed, or in error. What explains the two different numbers?
daily_puzzle.hint: Every actively traded stock actually carries two live prices at once, not one - and neither requires a trade to exist or to move.
daily_puzzle.solution: The two numbers were the bid and the ask: the highest price a buyer is currently offering, and the lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept.
daily_puzzle.explanation: A quoted price isn't one number - it's two prices in tension. Either side can move independently as traders revise their offers, with no trade required for that to happen. A trade only occurs when the two finally meet.

evening_quote.text: If you are distressed by anything external, the pain is not due to the thing itself, but to your estimate of it; and this you have the power to revoke at any moment.
